chain.g: a van, or fan for winnowing grain

ety.text: From Latin vannus (“a van, or fan for winnowing grain”): compare French van and English fan, winnow. Doublet of fan.

senses.d: A covered motor vehicle used to carry goods or (normally less than ten) persons, usually roughly cuboid in shape, Depending on the type of van, it can be bigger or smaller than a pickup truck and SUV, and longer and higher than a car but relatively smaller than a truck/lorry or a bus.
An enclosed railway vehicle for transport of goods, such as a boxcar/box van.
A light wagon, either covered or open, used by tradesmen and others for the transportation of goods.
A large towable vehicle equipped for the repair of structures that cannot easily be moved.
To transport in a van or similar vehicle (especially of horses).
ex: [They] had their own horses, but they hadn't bothered to van them over to Pine Hollow for this outing.

senses.d: Of law enforcement: to arrest (not necessarily in a van; derived from party van).
ex: Commander X: Yep, so now you all know how I got vanned. And you just met the snitch who did it to me.

senses.d: A shovel used in cleansing ore.
To wash or cleanse, as a small portion of ore, on a shovel.
A fan or other contrivance, such as a sieve, for winnowing grain.
ex: with strange amaze / A shepherd meeting thee, the oar surveys, / And names a van (Book XI)

senses.d: A wing with which the air is beaten.
ex: So Satan fell; and ſtrait a fiery Globe / Of Angels on full ſail of wing flew nigh, / Who on their plumy Vans receiv'd him ſoft […]
He wheeled in air, and stretched his vans in vain; / His vans no longer could his flight sustain.

grp.label: enclosed railway vehicle for transport of goods

From Middle English vandgard, vaunte garde, vaunt garde, wantgard, from advaunte-garde, avauntgard with aphesis, from Old French avangarde, avant-garde, avantgarde, from avant (“before; in front”) + garde (“guard”). Doublet of avant-garde and vaward.

senses.d: The leading units at the front of an army or fleet.
ex: They ſay, that the King diuided his Armie into three Battailes; whereof the Vant-guard onely well ſtrengthened with wings, came to fight.

senses.d: The person or people at the forefront of a group or movement.

grp.label: forefront of any group or movement

ety.text: Inherited from Old French avantgarde. By surface analysis, avant (“before, in front of”) + garde (“guard”).
From avan- + guardia.
Inherited from Old Spanish avanguardia, from aván, shortening of avante (“forward, ahead”) + guardia (“warden, guard”).

Old Catalan avantguardabor. Old Galician-Portuguese avanguardader. ▲ French avant-gardeinflu. Portuguese vanguarda Rebracketing of Old Galician-Portuguese avanguarda, reintepreting the initial ⟨a⟩ as the feminine definite article. Etymology 1 sense 2 is a semantic loan from French avant-garde.
Spanish vainillabor. English vanilla Borrowed from Spanish vainilla, a diminutive form of vaina (“pod”). "Plain" senses derive from the perceived plainness of vanilla ice cream.

senses.d: Any tropical climbing orchid of the genus Vanilla (especially Vanilla planifolia), bearing podlike fruit yielding an extract used in flavoring food or in perfumes.
ex: Vanilla itself was transplanted from Madagascar, the main source of the spice, to Polynesia a century ago.

senses.d: The fruit or bean of the vanilla plant.
The extract of the fruit of the vanilla plant.
The distinctive fragrant flavour/flavor characteristic of vanilla extract.
Any artificially produced homologue of vanilla extract, principally vanillin produced from lignin from the paper industry or from petrochemicals.
Someone who is not into fetishism.
An unmodded version of a game.
A yellowish-white colour, like that of vanilla ice cream.
A white person.
Of vanilla.
ex: A mass of folders and binders. One, vanilla in colour, catches her eye.

senses.d: Standard, plain, default, unmodified, basic.
Not kinky, not involving BDSM.
ex: While Dominick was more of a vanilla kind of a guy himself, he wasn't a total dunce when it came to the kinkier sides of things.
Sebastian could never do that, be in a marriage with a vanilla woman.

senses.d: Plain; conventional; unimaginative.
ex: a vanilla rendition of the concerto

ety.text: Borrowed from Spanish vainilla.
Borrowed from Spanish vainilla, a diminutive form of vaina.
From vaina (“pod”) + -illa (diminutive suffix).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bainilha, from Spanish vainilla.
From vainilla + -ado.
From va(i)n + -ity, from Middle English vanite, from Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas, from vānus, whence English vain. Doublet of vanitas.

senses.d: That which is vain, futile, or worthless; that which is of no value, use or profit.
Excessive pride in or admiration of one's own abilities, appearance, achievements, or possessions.
ex: It's not vanity, to me, it's my sanity

senses.d: A dressing table used to apply makeup, preen, and coif hair, in which the table is normally quite low and similar to a desk.
ex: She was sitting in front of her vanity, brushing out her hair.

senses.d: A washbasin installed into a permanently fixed storage unit, used as an item of bathroom furniture.
Any idea, theory or statement that is without foundation.
ex: It is a vanity to say that if two stones are dropped from a tower, the heavier will experience the greater acceleration.
To help the matter, the alchemists call in likewise many vanities out of astrology.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French vanité, from Old French, borrowed from Latin vānitātem.
From vano + -idad, or from Latin vānitātem, in this form probably borrowed. See also the older form vanedad.
From Old Galician-Portuguese vãidade, vãydade, from Latin vānitātem, from vānus. Compare vanidade, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vazio, from Latin vacīvus. Compare Galician and Spanish vacío.
Probably borrowed from Latin vānitātem.
